recording.starts: on the first onboarding screen with the name field already holding "Cameron"; any app launch or splash before it is not captured
recording.after_paywall: Two App Store purchases are cancelled, then Skip opens a "Pay what you want" slider sheet; Decline returns to the paywall, a second Skip lands on Home with one free escape, and a locked escape later opens a "50% off First-timer discount" sheet, which is declined.

strategy: Loóna runs onboarding as a short, warm conversation that turns a sleep problem into a taste profile. It greets the person by name, takes a bedtime target and their worries, explains the problem once in a three-card carousel (a wandering mind, a 47% statistic, a promised plan), then spends most of its questions on pleasant aesthetic choices (scenarios, colours, narratives) that make the product feel co-designed. A 40-second labelled loader names those very choices while reviews and a user count rotate below it, and ends on "Cameron, everything is ready" with a "Start my escape" button that opens the paywall instead. The carrying idea is personalisation as craft: you helped build this escape, so not opening it feels like leaving something of yours behind.

phases.name: Welcome by name
phases.goal: Make the first seconds feel like being greeted rather than processed: a name, pronouns and an age band, each one tap, so the person is invested and the app has a name to echo back later.

phases.name: Bedtime commitment
phases.goal: Have the person name a concrete bedtime target, a small commitment that the later plan promises to serve, and use that moment of intention to request notifications.

phases.name: Problem and promise
phases.goal: Turn the worries the person just picked into a common, blameless problem (a wandering mind), lend it authority with one statistic, and convert agreement into a request for a plan.

phases.name: Taste profile
phases.goal: Shift from problems to pleasures: the person co-designs their escapes by picking content, scenarios, colours and narratives, which feels creative and gives the coming loader something to visibly personalise; it closes with attribution framed as a favour.

phases.name: Building and reveal
phases.goal: Make a long wait feel like work being done on their own answers, fill it with social proof, then hand back a personal "everything is ready" so the paywall arrives as the gate to something already made for them.

phases.name: Paywall and exit offer
phases.goal: Convert at peak anticipation with a product demo, reviews, a pre-selected annual "welcome offer" priced per week and an opt-in trial; on Skip, try to recover the sale with a cheaper "Pay what you want" slider.

phases.name: Free taste and second discount
phases.goal: Let the person play one free escape under their own name, surround it with locked content, counters and referral rewards, and when they reach for a locked escape offer a deeper first-timer discount.

screens.title: Welcome to Loóna
screens.body: What do your friends call you?
screens.controls: Text field (filled: "Cameron"). Button: Continue. Top right: Skip
screens.visual: Near-black night sky with drifting purple star particles; "Loóna" in the accent purple; keyboard up; thin top progress bar just started; no back chevron on this first screen.
screens.intent: Opens with a greeting and asks for the name the way a friend would ("What do your friends call you?"), so the very first input is personal and almost effortless and gives the app a name to use later.

screens.title: Hi Cameron! How can we refer to you?
screens.body: We’re committed to creating a welcoming experience for members of all gender identities
screens.controls: Options: She / Her; He / Him; They / Them; Other (single select; He / Him picked). Button: Continue. Top: back chevron, Skip
screens.visual: "Hi Cameron!" in the accent purple, the first echo of the typed name; selected option gets a purple outline; progress bar a little further on.
screens.intent: Uses the name within a second of it being typed, proving the app is listening, and pairs it with an inclusivity line so the person feels welcome as who they are before any sleep question.

screens.title: Thanks! And how old are you?
screens.body: We’ll tweak our recommendations to show more content that we think you’ll like
screens.controls: Options: Less than 20; 20s; 30s; 40s; 50s; 60s (single select; 20s picked). Button: Continue
screens.visual: "how old" in purple; same dark list layout; progress bar about a sixth full.
screens.intent: A conversational "Thanks!" and a why-we-ask line make a demographic question feel like it serves the person (better recommendations) rather than the business.

screens.title: First, let’s set up your bedtime target
screens.body: Based on your target, Loóna will suggest you the best time to wind down for sleep
screens.controls: Time wheel (hours, minutes, am/pm), default 10:30 pm, changed to 10:00 pm. Button: Continue
screens.visual: "bedtime target" in purple; large rounded wheel card; progress bar about a quarter full.
screens.intent: Framed as "First", it gives the whole flow a concrete goal the person sets themselves; that number is what card 9 later promises to help them meet every night, and it quietly justifies the notification prompt that follows.

screens.title: “loóna” Would Like to Send You Notifications
screens.body: Notifications may include alerts, sounds, and icon badges. These can be configured in Settings.
screens.controls: Don’t Allow; Allow
screens.visual: System alert over the dimmed bedtime screen, fired on Continue after the bedtime was set; which button was tapped is not visible.
screens.intent: The bedtime screen behind it acts as the only primer: having just chosen a target and been told Loóna will suggest when to wind down, reminders feel like the obvious next step, so no separate explanation screen is spent.

screens.title: What’s on your mind before bed?
screens.body: Understanding yourself a little better will help you get the most out of Loóna
screens.controls: Options: Falling asleep faster; Reducing anxiety & stress; Relaxing my mind; Calming my thoughts; Reflecting on my day; Tucking my kids in (multi-select with check marks; first three picked). Button: Continue (disabled until a pick)
screens.visual: "before bed?" in purple; selected rows gain a purple outline and a check; progress bar about two fifths full.
screens.intent: Asks the person to name what keeps them up, framed as self-understanding; it sets up the carousel that follows, which speaks directly to a restless mind, and feeds the later Home line "Because your goal is to fall asleep faster".

screens.title: A wandering mind is not a happy mind
screens.body: Our unfocused mind easily gets stuck in a cycle of stressful and restless thoughts
screens.controls: Swipeable card, 3 dots. Button: Continue
screens.visual: Glowing neon line-art bear outline with a tangled ball of thread where its mind is; "not a happy mind" in purple; dots at 1 of 3. The person swiped back to this card once (0:31) before moving on.
screens.intent: Right after the worries question, it names the problem as a general mind habit ("Our unfocused mind"), so trouble switching off reads as normal and fixable rather than a personal failing; the soft mascot keeps the message gentle.

screens.title: We spend 47% of our time thinking about what isn’t going on
screens.controls: Swipeable card, 3 dots. Button: Continue
screens.visual: Neon line-art bear sitting with a honey jar over its head, small butterflies above and little creatures at its feet; "We spend 47% of our time" in purple; no source shown; dots at 2 of 3.
screens.intent: The flow’s single number gives the reframe weight and makes the person’s experience part of a near-universal pattern ("We"), which validates them and makes a product for it seem reasonable; it is presented without a citation.

screens.title: Let’s fix it and enjoy a good night’s sleep!
screens.body: Loóna will create a unique plan to help you meet your bedtime target every night
screens.controls: Swipeable card, 3 dots. Button: Personalize my plan (cross-fades from Continue on this card)
screens.visual: Neon line-art bed under a canopy with a lamp, alarm clock and book; "a good night’s sleep!" in purple; dots at 3 of 3.
screens.intent: Moves from problem to promise and ties it to the bedtime the person just set; changing the button to "Personalize my plan" makes their next tap an explicit request for the plan, which the following taste questions and loader then appear to fulfil.

screens.title: What kind of content do you find helpful?
screens.body: We’ll recommend more of the relevant content for your night-time
screens.controls: Options: Sleep stories; Sleep sounds; Music for sleep; Breathing exercises (check marks; Sleep stories picked). Button: Continue
screens.visual: "you find helpful?" in purple; progress bar a little past halfway.
screens.intent: First of the "personalize my plan" questions, it keeps the promise just made by asking what format the person wants.

screens.title: Choose one or more scenarios you like
screens.body: We’ll tweak our recommendations to show more content that we think you’ll like
screens.controls: Options: Nature getaways; Cozy interiors; Everyday magic; Fantasy; Myths and history; Nostalgia (multi-select; Nature getaways picked). Button: Continue (disabled until a pick)
screens.visual: "scenarios" in purple; same list style; progress bar about two thirds.
screens.intent: Turns the flow from problems to pleasant choices, so answering feels like browsing a catalogue of places the person would like to escape to.

screens.subtype: taste: colour swatches (pick at least three)
screens.title: Choose three or more colors you like
screens.body: We’ll tweak our recommendations to show more content that we think you’ll like
screens.controls: Grid of 21 colour circles in 7 rows of 3 (purples, oranges, yellows, pinks, reds, teals, blues), scrollable; picked circles grow and show a check (dark purple, dark teal, dark blue picked). Button: Continue (disabled until three are picked)
screens.visual: "colors" in purple; full-bleed swatch grid that scrolls under the header; Continue lights up on the third pick.
screens.intent: A playful, almost tactile choice that has nothing to do with sleep problems but makes the product feel hand-made for the person; the minimum of three adds a little effort that later reads as "my colour palette" in the loader.

screens.title: Choose one or more narratives you like
screens.body: We’ll tweak our recommendations to show more content that we think you’ll like
screens.controls: Options: Realistic; Mysterious; Fairy-tale; Nostalgic; Sentimental; Adventure (multi-select; Mysterious picked). Button: Continue
screens.visual: "narratives" in purple; progress bar about four fifths.
screens.intent: Completes the creative brief (format, setting, colour, story tone) so the person has authored a full profile for the loader to "apply".

screens.title: Lastly, how did you hear about Loóna?
screens.body: It’ll help us to improve our marketing magic and let more people have better sleep
screens.controls: Options: Social media; Online ad; Friend or family; App Store or Google Play; News, article or blog; Therapist or sleep professional; Other (single select; Online ad picked). Button: Continue
screens.visual: "hear about Loóna?" in purple; progress bar nearly full.
screens.intent: "Lastly" signals the end so the person pushes through, and the business question is framed as helping other people sleep, a small favour asked after the app has promised them a plan.

intermission_pattern: Loóna has very few pure intermissions: one three-card carousel (screens 7 to 9) placed after the fifth question, directly after the multi-select "What’s on your mind before bed?" and before the taste questions, so about one intermission block per ten questions. The cards are short (a headline with a purple key phrase and at most one sentence), drawn as glowing line-art bears, and step from problem (a wandering mind) to evidence (47%) to promise (a unique plan for your bedtime target), with the last button turning into "Personalize my plan". Elsewhere the intermission work is folded into the questions themselves: conversational openers ("Hi Cameron!", "Thanks!", "First,", "Lastly,") and why-we-ask lines ("We’ll tweak our recommendations...") keep a feeling of dialogue without extra screens. The heavy persuasion is saved for the end, where a 40-second loader doubles as a social-proof wall and a one-line personal reveal cashes in everything the carousel promised and the taste questions invested.
standouts: Screen 9 swaps the carousel’s Continue for "Personalize my plan", so the person’s next tap is a request for the plan rather than agreement with a slide, a neat commitment step just before the taste questions.

Screen 15 names its four bars after the person’s own inputs (Color palette, Visual setting, Sleep sounds, Narrative preference) with busy verbs and percentages, so 40 seconds of waiting reads as tailoring, while an unverifiable "Trusted by over 114,058 people" and named, aged, located reviews fill the wait.

Screen 8 is the flow’s only statistic and carries no source on screen, though it matches Killingsworth and Gilbert’s 2010 finding that people mind-wander about 47% of the time, and screen 7’s headline paraphrases that paper’s title, "A wandering mind is an unhappy mind".

The name is used sparingly and always in the accent purple: "Hi Cameron!" a second after it is typed (screen 2), then not again until "Cameron, everything is ready" (screen 16) and "Daily picks for Cameron" on Home (screen 19), bookending the flow.
gaps: The recording starts on the name screen with "Cameron" already typed, so any launch or splash screen is not shown. Whether Allow or Don’t Allow was tapped on the notification prompt is not visible. The paywall and loader review cards rotate, so only the cards that appeared are transcribed. The App Store purchase sheets and "Unable to purchase" alerts are folded into the paywall entry, and the account email on those sheets is left out on purpose. Post-paywall screens are summarised in three app entries plus the second discount sheet. "other" counts the paywall, the two discount sheets and the three app entries. No new mechanism names were added.
